lines.text: Ocean voyagers, sacred kings and the only Pacific kingdom never colonised. This is the story of Tonga, from its first settlers to a mighty eruption.
More than three thousand years ago, the Lapita people, makers of finely decorated pottery, sailed east and first settled these islands.
Their descendants became master navigators, crossing open ocean in double canoes, guided only by stars, swells, winds and birds.
By the tenth century the Tui Tonga, sacred kings, ruled an ocean empire whose reach stretched to Samoa and Fiji.
Around 1200 a Tui Tonga raised the Haamonga a Maui, a great gate of three stones that still stands today.
In the 1770s the British navigator James Cook visited, on his voyages across the Pacific.
Before the century was out, Nukualofa was founded, the town that would become the capital.
George Tupou the First, born in 1797, would unite the islands and give Tonga a constitution.
In 1845 he united Tonga as one kingdom, some one hundred and seventy islands, never to be colonised.
Queen Salote Tupou the Third reigned for almost half a century, and was loved around the world for riding in the rain at the coronation of 1953.
In 1959 Tupou the Sixth was born. He would become king in 2012, after Tonga was fully independent and more democratic.
In 2006 riots for democracy swept the capital, and much of its centre burned.
Then in January 2022 an undersea volcano exploded, the largest eruption of the century so far, sending a tsunami across the islands.
From sacred kings to a kingdom that rebuilt after the blast, Tonga remains proudly its own.
